title: The Lacoste crocodile
hook: The crocodile on Lacoste shirts was a tennis champion's nickname.
peek: René Lacoste was a French tennis champion of the 1920s nicknamed the Crocodile. When he began making shirts in 1933, he put the animal on the chest, one of the earliest logos worn on the outside of clothes.
lede: René Lacoste won seven Grand Slam singles titles in the 1920s and was one of France's Four Musketeers of tennis. American newspapers called him the Alligator, and in France this became the Crocodile. In 1933 he co-founded a company to make his tennis shirts, with a small crocodile embroidered on the chest where everyone could see it.

bullets.text: The story usually told is that in 1923, on a Davis Cup trip to Boston, his team captain promised him an alligator-skin suitcase if he won an important match. He lost, but the press picked up the tale, and the nickname followed.
Lacoste's friend Robert George drew a crocodile, which Lacoste had stitched onto the blazer he wore to matches. When the shirts went on sale, the same emblem went with them.

Players then often wore long-sleeved woven shirts. Lacoste's design had short sleeves, a soft ribbed collar and breathable knitted cotton called piqué, with a longer tail at the back to stay tucked in.
Makers' names had usually been hidden on labels inside clothes. Putting the crocodile on the chest is often cited as one of the first examples of a visible brand logo on clothing.
